posts.title: RAG or Fine-Tuning: Choosing the Right Approach for Your Business Data
posts.excerpt: Retrieval teaches a model what to know at the moment of answering. Fine-tuning teaches it how to behave. Most business AI needs retrieval first, and fine-tuning only for specific jobs.
posts.content:
Use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) when an AI system must answer from facts that change or must be cited, such as policies, product data, contracts and past work. Use fine-tuning when you need a model to follow a consistent style, format or specialised task that prompting alone cannot achieve. For most business applications, RAG is the foundation, and fine-tuning is an optional refinement.

The two are often confused because both involve "your data". They do very different jobs.

## What each approach does

**RAG** keeps your knowledge in documents and databases. When a question arrives, the system retrieves the most relevant passages and gives them to the model as context. The model answers using that material, and can show where each point came from.

**Fine-tuning** adjusts the model's internal weights by training it on examples of inputs and desired outputs. The model learns patterns: tone, structure, classification rules, domain vocabulary.

A useful way to think about it: RAG is an open-book exam; fine-tuning is practice until the habits stick.

## Comparison

| Factor | RAG | Fine-tuning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best for | Facts, documents, changing information | Style, format, narrow repeated tasks |
| Updating knowledge | Edit the documents | Retrain the model |
| Showing sources | Yes | No |
| Removing information | Immediate | Requires retraining |
| Data needed | Your existing documents | Hundreds to thousands of curated examples |
| Risk of confident errors | Lower, when well built | Higher for factual questions |
| Upfront effort | Moderate | Higher |

## When RAG is the right choice

- Internal knowledge assistants for HR, IT and operations.
- Customer support answering from product and policy documents.
- Sales teams searching past proposals and specifications.
- Any use where answers must be traceable to a source.

## When fine-tuning adds value

- **Consistent output format:** for example, turning messy notes into a structured report every time.
- **Classification at scale:** routing tickets, tagging documents or scoring leads with your own categories.
- **Domain language:** specialised terminology where a general model stumbles.
- **Smaller, cheaper models:** fine-tuning a small model on a narrow task can match a large model's accuracy at lower running cost, which matters for on-premise deployment.

## Combining the two

Many strong systems use both: a fine-tuned model that follows your format and terminology, answering from content retrieved by RAG. Start with RAG, measure accuracy on a test set of real questions, and add fine-tuning only where the measurements show a gap that prompting cannot close.

## A worked example

Consider a distributor with 4,000 products, frequent price changes and a sales team that answers dealer questions all day.

- **With RAG only:** product sheets, price lists and policy documents are indexed. A salesperson asks, "What is the current price and lead time for item X in the 25 kg pack?" The system retrieves today's price list and the item sheet, answers, and links both. When prices change on Monday, the new list is indexed and answers change immediately.
- **With fine-tuning only:** the model would learn prices from training examples. By Monday it would be out of date, and nobody could tell which answers were stale.
- **With both:** RAG supplies the facts, while a lightly fine-tuned model formats every reply in the house style dealers expect, with pack size, price, lead time and minimum order always in the same order.

The example shows the general rule: facts come from retrieval, habits from fine-tuning.

## Data security considerations

With RAG, your documents stay in your own storage and access controls can follow the user, so a staff member only retrieves what they are allowed to see. With fine-tuning, information becomes part of the model, which makes it harder to restrict or remove. For sensitive data, this is a strong argument for RAG.

## A practical path

1. Pick one use case and one document set.
2. Build a RAG prototype and a test set of 50 to 100 real questions.
3. Measure accuracy, citations and refusals.
4. Fix data gaps first; they cause most errors.
5. Consider fine-tuning only for remaining format or task problems.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can we fine-tune a model on our documents so it knows them?

You can, but it is an unreliable way to store facts, and the model cannot cite sources. RAG is better for knowledge.

### Does RAG work with Hindi documents?

Yes. Modern embedding models and language models handle Hindi and mixed Hindi-English content.

### Which is cheaper?

RAG is usually cheaper to start and maintain. Fine-tuning can reduce running costs later by allowing a smaller model for a narrow task.

### Can both run on our own servers?

Yes. Open models support both approaches in private cloud or on-premise environments.

## Choose the approach that fits your data

Turbo Bytes Consulting designs [AI applications](/services/ai-applications) and [custom LLM systems](/services/custom-llm) using retrieval, fine-tuning or both. For a step-by-step view, read [how to build an AI chatbot on your company documents](/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-chatbot-trained-on-your-company-documents).

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) to discuss your data and your use case.

posts.title: How Much Does a Business Website Cost in India
posts.excerpt: A business website in India can cost from under ₹1 lakh to well over ₹10 lakh. The difference lies in content, custom functionality and how seriously the site is built to win enquiries.
posts.content:
A business website in India typically costs under ₹1 lakh for a template-based brochure site, ₹2 lakh to ₹6 lakh for a custom-designed B2B site built to generate enquiries, and ₹6 lakh or more when it includes custom functionality such as client portals, calculators or integrations. What moves the price is content, design depth, functionality and the care taken over search and conversion.

## The three tiers

| Type | What you get | Indicative range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Template brochure site | 5 to 10 pages on a purchased theme, basic contact form | Under ₹1 lakh |
| Custom B2B site | Custom design, 15 to 30 pages, service pages, case studies, blog, SEO and tracking | ₹2 lakh to ₹6 lakh |
| Site with web application features | Client portal, pricing calculator, booking, CRM or ERP integration | ₹6 lakh and above |

These are planning ranges for professional work, not quotes.

## What drives the price

### Content

Content is the most underestimated cost. Service pages, case studies and about pages need writing, and good B2B copy needs someone who understands your business. If you supply finished copy, the price falls; if the agency writes it, expect it to be a significant part of the budget and worth it.

### Design depth

A template adjusted with your colours is quick. A custom design system, with page layouts created for your content and brand, takes longer and usually converts better.

### Functionality

Each custom feature adds cost: multi-step forms, calculators, gated downloads, portals, multilingual content, or integrations with your CRM and email tools.

### Platform

WordPress with a theme is quickest for simple sites. Modern frameworks such as Next.js cost more upfront for simple sites but less for sites with custom features. See [Next.js vs WordPress](/blog/nextjs-vs-wordpress-for-a-business-website-in-2026).

### Search and conversion work

Keyword research, page structure, metadata, schema markup, speed optimisation and conversion tracking. Skipping these makes a site cheaper and much less useful.

## Ongoing costs

- **Domain and hosting:** usually a small annual amount for business sites.
- **Maintenance:** updates, security patches and small edits. Often a monthly retainer.
- **Content:** new blog posts, case studies and page updates keep a B2B site ranking and relevant.

## How to compare website quotes

Quotes for the "same" website can differ several times over. To compare them fairly, ask each agency to state:

- **Number of unique page designs,** not just total pages. Ten pages built from two templates cost far less than ten custom layouts.
- **Who writes the content,** and how many rounds of revision are included.
- **What SEO work is included:** keyword mapping, metadata, schema, redirects from the old site.
- **Which integrations are included:** CRM, email marketing, WhatsApp, analytics.
- **Testing:** which browsers and devices.
- **Training and handover:** how your team will edit the site.
- **What happens after launch:** warranty period for defects and the cost of ongoing support.

Put the answers in a table. Most price gaps turn out to be scope gaps.

## What a cheap website usually leaves out

- Proper redirects when replacing an old site, which protects rankings.
- Mobile testing across real devices.
- Speed optimisation and image compression.
- Analytics and conversion tracking.
- Accessibility and security basics.
- Source files and admin access in your name.

Each omission costs more to fix later than to include at the start.

## How to budget

Work back from value. If one new client is worth several lakh to your business, a site that reliably generates a few qualified enquiries a month justifies a serious budget. If the site is mainly a credibility check for referrals, a smaller investment is reasonable.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long does a business website take?

Template sites take two to four weeks. Custom B2B sites typically take six to ten weeks, with content as the usual bottleneck.

### Should we pay monthly or once?

Both models exist. Paying once for the build and separately for maintenance keeps ownership clear.

### Do we own the website?

You should own the domain, hosting account, design files and code. Confirm this in writing before starting.

### Can we update the site ourselves?

Yes, with a CMS. Ask for training and a short guide as part of the project.

## Plan a website that pays for itself

Turbo Bytes Consulting builds [B2B websites and web applications](/services/web-development) designed to win enquiries. Before you start, work through our [website redesign checklist](/blog/website-redesign-checklist-for-b2b-companies).

posts.title: Tally Integration: Connecting Your Accounts to Your Operations Software
posts.excerpt: Most Indian SMEs keep their books in Tally and run operations elsewhere. Connecting the two removes double entry, speeds up invoicing and lets everyone see payment status without calling accounts.
posts.content:
Integrating Tally with your operations software means customers, items, invoices and payment status flow automatically between accounts and the systems your sales and operations teams use, so nothing is typed twice. It is usually done through Tally's built-in XML interface or a connector running alongside Tally, with clear rules about which system owns each type of data.

## Why it matters

In a typical growing business:

- Sales creates an order in a CRM or spreadsheet.
- Accounts re-enters it in Tally to raise the invoice.
- Salespeople call accounts to ask whether a customer has paid.
- Month-end reports combine exports from both, by hand.

Every manual step adds delay and errors. Integration removes them.

## What to sync

| Data | Usually owned by | Direction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customer and supplier masters | Operations or CRM | To Tally |
| Item and stock masters | Tally or ERP | Depends on setup |
| Sales orders and invoices | Operations system | To Tally |
| Receipts and outstanding balances | Tally | From Tally |
| Purchase bills | Operations or procurement | To Tally |
| GST details | Tally | Both, validated |

The key decision is ownership. Each piece of data should be created in one place and copied, never edited in both.

## How the integration works

- **Tally's XML interface.** Tally can accept and return data through requests sent to it over the local network. Custom software can create vouchers, read ledgers and pull reports this way.
- **Connector service.** A small program runs on the machine or server where Tally lives, collects changes, and syncs them with your cloud software on a schedule.
- **Tally on cloud hosting.** When Tally is hosted remotely, the same methods apply, with attention to network access and security.

For most SMEs, a connector with scheduled sync every few minutes gives near-real-time data without the complexity of instant updates.

## What changes for each team

**Sales** sees each customer's outstanding balance and overdue invoices before calling them, and stops asking accounts for updates.

**Accounts** stops re-typing orders. Their work shifts to checking exceptions the integration flags, such as a missing GSTIN or a customer not yet matched.

**Operations** knows which orders are invoiced and which are held for payment, so dispatch decisions are faster.

**Leadership** gets daily figures for sales, collections and receivables without waiting for month-end.

The integration is only successful if each team trusts the numbers. Run old and new processes side by side for two to four weeks, compare the results daily, and switch over only when they match.

## Common pitfalls

- **Master data mismatches.** A customer spelt differently in two systems creates duplicates. Clean and match masters before going live.
- **GST and tax details.** Invoices must carry correct GSTINs, HSN codes and tax splits. Validate before sending to Tally.
- **Editing in both places.** If accounts edits an invoice in Tally that operations created, the systems drift apart. Agree who corrects what.
- **Tally not running.** If the connector depends on Tally being open, plan for when the machine is off. Queues and retry logic prevent lost data.

## A phased plan

1. **Map data and ownership** with accounts and operations together.
2. **Clean and match masters.** Customers, suppliers and items.
3. **Phase 1: invoices to Tally.** The biggest time saver.
4. **Phase 2: payments back.** Outstanding balances visible to sales.
5. **Phase 3: reporting.** Combined operational and financial dashboards.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does Tally integration require replacing Tally?

No. The point is to keep Tally for accounts and compliance while connecting it to operational systems.

### Can a CRM like Zoho or HubSpot connect to Tally?

Yes, through connectors or custom integration. Custom CRMs can connect directly. See [Custom CRM vs Zoho vs HubSpot](/blog/custom-crm-vs-zoho-vs-hubspot-for-indian-smes).

### Is the data secure?

It can be. Keep the connector on your network, encrypt data in transit, and limit which ledgers the integration can read or write.

### How long does it take?

A focused invoice and payment sync typically takes three to six weeks, including master data clean-up and testing with your accounts team.

## Connect your accounts to your operations

Turbo Bytes Consulting builds Tally integrations as part of our [business automation services](/services/business-automation), linking accounts with CRM, ERP and [custom software](/services/custom-software-development).

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) and we will map what should sync in your business.

posts.title: Software for Manufacturing Companies in Noida
posts.excerpt: Noida's manufacturers run on Tally, Excel and phone calls longer than they should. The highest-return software is usually not a full ERP but targeted systems for quotations, production tracking and dispatch.
posts.content:
For manufacturing companies in Noida and Greater Noida, the software that pays back fastest is usually targeted: a quotation system for engineered products, production and job tracking on the shop floor, inventory and dispatch visibility, and integration with Tally. A full ERP can come later, or may not be needed at all if these pieces are connected well.

Noida's industrial phases and Greater Noida's sectors host manufacturers of electronics, auto components, garments, packaging, engineering goods and more. Many have grown to 50 to 300 people while their systems stayed at the 20-person stage.

## Where manufacturers lose time

- **Quotations** built in Excel from old files, checked by one senior engineer, taking days.
- **Production status** known only by walking the floor or calling the supervisor.
- **Inventory** that differs between the store register, Tally and reality.
- **Dispatch** planned on WhatsApp, with customers calling for updates.
- **Quality records** on paper, hard to retrieve when a customer complains.
- **Reports** assembled by hand for the monthly review.

## Software that helps most

### Quotation and costing

Rules-based quotation tools calculate prices from materials, processes and margins, and generate consistent documents. For engineering manufacturers, this can turn a two-day task into an hour and reduce pricing errors.

### Production and job tracking

Simple screens or tablets at workstations record job start, completion, rejections and downtime. Managers see work in progress live, and planners know what is really late.

### Inventory and stores

Barcode-based receipts and issues keep stock accurate. Reorder alerts prevent shortages that stop production.

### Dispatch and delivery

Dispatch planning linked to orders, with automatic WhatsApp updates to customers and proof of delivery from drivers.

### Quality

Digital inspection checklists with photos, linked to jobs and batches, so traceability takes minutes.

### Accounts integration

All of the above connected to Tally, so invoices, stock values and receivables stay consistent. Read our guide to [Tally integration](/blog/tally-integration-connecting-your-accounts-to-your-operations-software).

## Where to start

Pick the area where delay or error costs the most money:

- Losing orders to slow quotes? Start with quotations.
- Missing delivery dates? Start with production tracking.
- Frequent stock-outs or write-offs? Start with inventory.

Deliver that first, prove the benefit, then connect the next piece.

## Build, buy or customise?

Some manufacturers fit a packaged ERP well; others have processes too distinctive for it. Our guide to [ERP for manufacturing SMEs](/blog/erp-for-manufacturing-smes-build-buy-or-customise) explains how to decide.

## Measuring the return

Before building anything, record the current numbers for the area you are fixing, so the benefit is visible afterwards:

- **Quotations:** average time from enquiry to quote sent, and the win rate.
- **Production:** percentage of jobs delivered on the promised date, and hours lost to waiting for materials or information.
- **Inventory:** stock-outs per month and the value of write-offs at stock-take.
- **Dispatch:** customer calls asking for delivery status.
- **Reporting:** hours spent preparing the monthly review.

Measure the same numbers three months after go-live. This keeps the project honest and makes the case for the next phase.

## Adoption on the shop floor

Software fails in factories when it is designed for offices. Good shop-floor systems:

- Use large buttons, few fields and local language labels where helpful.
- Work on inexpensive tablets or phones.
- Cope with patchy Wi-Fi.
- Save supervisors time rather than adding reporting work.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do we need a full ERP?

Not always. Many manufacturers get most of the benefit from connected, targeted systems plus Tally, at lower cost and risk.

### Can workers without computer experience use it?

Yes, if screens are designed for them. Simple, visual interfaces on tablets work well on the shop floor.

### How long does a first module take?

Two to four months for a focused module such as quotations or production tracking, including testing on the floor.

### Can a local partner visit our factory?

Yes. Discovery works best on site, watching how work actually moves.

## Software for your factory

We serve clients across [Delhi NCR](/software-development-company-delhi-ncr).

posts.title: The Founder Dependency Test: Can Your Business Run Without You
posts.excerpt: If the business slows every time you step away, it is not a team problem. It is a design problem. Ten questions show where the dependency sits and what to fix first.
posts.content:
A business is founder-dependent when decisions, customer relationships or critical knowledge sit with one person, so work slows or stops when that person is unavailable. The test below scores ten common dependencies. Most founders of companies with 30 to 300 people find three or four of them, and fixing them usually takes months, not years.

Dependency is rarely a sign of a weak team. It is usually a sign that the business grew faster than its processes, and the founder filled every gap personally.

## The ten questions

Answer yes or no to each.

1. **Could the business run for two weeks without you checking your phone?**
2. **Do pricing and discount decisions happen without you?**
3. **Do your largest clients have strong relationships with at least two other people in the company?**
4. **Is there a written record of how your core processes work?**
5. **Can your managers see the numbers they need without asking you or accounts?**
6. **Are hiring decisions for roles below senior management made without you?**
7. **Do department heads resolve disagreements between themselves most of the time?**
8. **Could someone else run the weekly leadership meeting?**
9. **Are supplier and vendor relationships held by people other than you?**
10. **Is critical knowledge, such as technical specifications, costing logic and key contacts, stored somewhere other than your head and your inbox?**

## Reading your score

- **8 to 10 yes:** the business is largely independent. Your focus can move to strategy and growth.
- **5 to 7 yes:** partial dependency. Pick the two weakest areas and fix them this quarter.
- **4 or fewer:** high dependency. The business's growth is capped by your time. This is the most urgent problem to address.

## What each "no" usually means

**Pricing and discounts (2).** Without clear rules, every quote comes to you. Write pricing guidelines with approval limits, and let a system enforce them.

**Client relationships (3).** Introduce a second senior contact to every major client, and share account notes in a CRM rather than in your WhatsApp.

**Process records (4).** Document the few processes that matter most, starting with order to delivery. Short, current and owned by someone.

**Information access (5).** A leadership dashboard fed automatically from accounts, sales and operations removes a large share of the questions that reach you.

**Knowledge storage (10).** This is the hidden risk. Specifications, costing logic and history stored in one person's head or email are a single point of failure for the whole company.

## The role of systems

Most founder dependency is not about authority. It is about information. People come to the founder because the founder knows. Three kinds of system change that:

- **Workflow tools** that route approvals by rule, so only exceptions need you.
- **Dashboards** that show every manager the same, current numbers.
- **Knowledge systems,** including AI assistants trained on company documents, that make expertise available to everyone. See [how to build an AI chatbot on your company documents](/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-chatbot-trained-on-your-company-documents).

## A 90-day plan to reduce dependency

1. **Weeks 1 to 2:** take the test with your leadership team and compare answers.
2. **Weeks 3 to 6:** write approval rules for pricing, purchases and hiring. Delegate within them.
3. **Weeks 7 to 10:** put the key numbers on one dashboard and start an [operating rhythm](/blog/the-operating-rhythm-reviews-that-keep-a-growing-company-on-track).
4. **Weeks 11 to 13:** take a week away, deliberately, and review what came back to you.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is some founder dependency healthy?

Yes. Vision, culture and the largest strategic relationships should stay with the founder. The aim is to remove dependency on routine decisions and information.

### Why does delegation fail in growing companies?

Usually because people are given tasks without the authority, information or rules to decide. Delegating authority, not just tasks, is the difference.

### Should we hire before reducing dependency?

Often the order is reversed: clear processes and information make new senior hires effective much faster.

### How does this affect company valuation?

Buyers and investors discount businesses that depend on one person. Reducing dependency usually increases value.

## Find where your business depends on you

Turbo Bytes Consulting's [Business Diagnostic](/services) identifies founder dependencies and the processes and systems that remove them. Where systems are needed, we build them through [business automation](/services/business-automation).

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) and bring your test results.

posts.title: Building a Field Sales App for Your Team
posts.excerpt: A good field sales app replaces calls, WhatsApp photos and end-of-day reports with one simple tool that works offline. Here are the features that matter, and the ones that can wait.
posts.content:
A field sales app gives salespeople one place on their phone to see their daily plan, check in at visits, record orders, photos and notes, and sync everything to the office, even when there is no signal. For managers it replaces phone calls and end-of-day WhatsApp reports with a live view of the team's activity and pipeline.

Many Indian companies with dealer, distributor or retail networks still run field sales on calls, spreadsheets and photos sent over WhatsApp. The information arrives late, in different formats, and is hard to analyse.

## Must-have features

### Daily plan and beat

Each salesperson sees the customers and dealers they should visit today, with addresses, last order, outstanding balance and notes from previous visits.

### Check-in with location

A one-tap check-in records time and GPS location. Managers see coverage without asking.

### Order capture

A simple catalogue with prices, schemes and stock availability. Orders flow straight to the office and, where connected, to your ERP or Tally.

### Notes, photos and follow-ups

Shelf photos, competitor information and follow-up tasks captured in the moment, attached to the right customer.

### Offline mode

The app must work in basements, markets and industrial areas with poor coverage, and sync when a connection returns. This is non-negotiable for field use in India.

### Manager dashboard

Visits planned against completed, orders by person and territory, new customers, and overdue follow-ups.

## Features that can wait

- Route optimisation.
- Gamification and leaderboards.
- AI-generated visit suggestions.
- Expense claims.

Useful, but none of them matter if the basics are not adopted first.

## Integrations

| System | What it adds |
| --- | --- |
| CRM | Customer history and pipeline |
| Tally or ERP | Prices, stock, invoices, outstanding balances |
| WhatsApp Business | Order confirmations to dealers |
| Maps | Directions and territory views |

Integration with accounts is especially valuable: salespeople who can see a dealer's overdue balance collect more and promise less. Read our guide to [Tally integration](/blog/tally-integration-connecting-your-accounts-to-your-operations-software).

## Designing for adoption

Field apps fail when they feel like surveillance or add work. To avoid that:

- **Make it faster than the old way.** If placing an order takes longer in the app than on a call, people will call.
- **Give salespeople something back:** customer history, outstanding balances, their own targets and incentives.
- **Keep forms short.** Three taps for a check-in, not ten fields.
- **Involve two or three top salespeople** in testing before rollout.
- **Train in the field,** not in a conference room.

## A rollout plan that works

1. **Pilot with one territory for three weeks.** Choose a manager who wants it to succeed and a mix of strong and average salespeople.
2. **Fix what they complain about.** Early feedback is usually about speed, missing products or confusing scheme rules. Solve these before expanding.
3. **Stop accepting orders by phone in the pilot territory.** Parallel channels kill adoption; once the app works, make it the only route.
4. **Expand territory by territory,** with a short field training session for each.
5. **Review adoption weekly** for the first two months: visits logged, orders in the app, sync failures.

Rolling out to the whole team on day one usually produces a flood of small problems and a loss of trust that is hard to recover.

## Build or buy?

Packaged field-force apps exist and suit standard needs. A custom app makes sense when your pricing, schemes, product configuration or dealer structure is complex, or when you want tight integration with your own systems. See [React Native vs Flutter vs native](/blog/react-native-vs-flutter-vs-native-in-2026) for the technology choice.

## Cost and timeline

A focused field sales app with plan, check-in, orders, offline sync and a manager dashboard typically takes 10 to 14 weeks. Costs sit in the middle band described in our guide to [mobile app development cost in India](/blog/mobile-app-development-cost-in-india-what-drives-the-price).

## Frequently asked questions

### Will salespeople accept location tracking?

They generally accept check-in location at visits. Continuous tracking is more sensitive; explain the purpose and limit it to working hours.

### Can it work on low-cost Android phones?

Yes. Design and test for the phones your team actually carries.

### How do we handle schemes and discounts?

Encode them as rules in the app, with approval requests for exceptions, so salespeople quote correctly without calling the office.

### What is the first thing to measure?

Visits logged per salesperson per day and orders captured in the app versus by phone. Adoption comes before any other metric.

## Equip your field team

Turbo Bytes Consulting builds [mobile apps](/services/mobile-app-development) for field sales and service teams, connected to your [business systems](/services/business-automation).

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) and tell us how your team sells today.

posts.title: What a Software Requirements Document Should Contain Before You Hire a Developer
posts.excerpt: A clear requirements document is the cheapest insurance in any software project. It does not need to be long. It needs to describe the business, the users, the rules and what done looks like.
posts.content:
A software requirements document should describe the business problem, the users and their roles, the workflows step by step, the business rules and exceptions, the systems it must connect to, the data it will hold, and how you will judge that it works. Ten to twenty clear pages are enough for most business systems, and they make quotes comparable and projects predictable.

You do not need to be technical to write one. You need to know how your business works, which is exactly what developers do not know.

## 1. Purpose and goals

One page. What problem are you solving, and how will you know it is solved? Use measurable outcomes: quotation time down from two days to two hours; no orders typed twice; month-end report ready on the first working day.

## 2. Users and roles

List every type of user and what they need to do:

| Role | Main tasks | Sees | Can approve |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sales executive | Create quotes and orders | Own customers | Discounts up to 5 percent |
| Sales manager | Review pipeline | Team's customers | Discounts up to 15 percent |
| Accounts | Invoice, record payments | All financial data | Credit limits |

Roles and permissions drive a large share of development effort, so be specific.

## 3. Workflows

Describe each workflow as numbered steps, from trigger to outcome. For example: enquiry received, quote prepared, quote approved, quote sent, order confirmed, order passed to production.

For each step, note who does it, what information they need, and what happens next.

## 4. Business rules and exceptions

This is where projects succeed or fail. Write down:

- Calculation rules, such as pricing, taxes, commissions.
- Approval limits and who can override them.
- What happens when someone is on leave.
- What happens when a customer changes an order after confirmation.
- Cancellations, returns, partial deliveries.

The exceptions you forget to mention become change requests later.

## 5. Integrations

List every system the software must talk to, what data moves, in which direction, and how often: Tally, CRM, payment gateway, WhatsApp, email, existing databases. Note whether each system has an API or only exports files.

## 6. Data

- What records the system will hold, such as customers, products, orders and documents.
- What existing data must be migrated, and where it lives now.
- How long data must be retained, and any privacy requirements under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

## 7. Reports and dashboards

List the reports people need, who needs them and how often. Attach examples of the spreadsheets you use today; they are often the best specification.

## 8. Non-functional requirements

- Expected number of users and records.
- Mobile or desktop use, and whether offline access is needed.
- Security expectations, such as two-factor login.
- Availability, such as business hours or around the clock.

## 9. Acceptance criteria

For each workflow, describe how you will test that it works: "A sales executive can create a quote for a configured product in under five minutes, and it matches the price the current spreadsheet calculates."

## 10. What is out of scope

Listing what you are not building now prevents misunderstandings and keeps the first phase focused.

## A shortcut: paid discovery

If writing this feels daunting, many development partners offer a short discovery phase in which they interview your team and produce the document with you. It usually costs a small fraction of the project and produces a better result than either side working alone.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long should the document be?

Long enough to answer the questions above clearly. For most business systems, ten to twenty pages plus screenshots of current spreadsheets.

### Should we include screen designs?

Rough sketches help. Detailed designs usually come later, from the development partner.

### Who should write it?

The person who owns the process, with input from the people who do the work every day.

### Will developers still have questions?

Yes, and that is good. A clear document makes the questions better and fewer.

## Start with clarity

Turbo Bytes Consulting runs discovery phases that turn your knowledge of the business into a clear specification and a fixed price. See our [custom software development services](/services/custom-software-development) and our guide on [how to choose a development company](/blog/how-to-choose-a-software-development-company-in-noida-12-questions-to-ask).

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) and we will tell you what your specification needs to cover.

posts.title: AI Chatbots for Universities and Colleges: Admissions, Queries and Student Support
posts.excerpt: Admissions teams answer the same questions thousands of times each season. An AI assistant trained on a university's own information can answer them instantly, in English and Hindi, and pass serious enquiries to counsellors.
posts.content:
An AI chatbot for a university or college answers prospective and current students' questions about courses, eligibility, fees, deadlines, hostels and procedures, using the institution's own documents, around the clock and in English or Hindi. It captures enquiries as leads for the admissions team and hands complex or sensitive cases to a counsellor.

For Indian institutions, the admissions season brings a surge of repetitive questions across phone, email, website and WhatsApp. Staff spend their days answering "What is the last date?" and "Is there a hostel?" while serious applicants wait.

## What the chatbot handles

**For prospective students and parents:**

- Course details, eligibility, entrance requirements and seat availability.
- Fee structures, scholarships and payment options.
- Application steps, documents required and important dates.
- Campus facilities, hostels and transport.

**For current students:**

- Timetables, examination rules and results procedures.
- Fee payment status and deadlines.
- Library, hostel and administrative procedures.

**For staff:**

- Quick answers on internal policies and procedures.

## How it works

The assistant is built on the institution's prospectus, fee notices, regulations, FAQs and website content. When someone asks a question, it retrieves the relevant passages and answers from them, citing the source. If the answer is not in the material, it says so and offers a counsellor. See [how document-based chatbots work](/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-chatbot-trained-on-your-company-documents).

## Channels

- **Website chat** on course and admissions pages.
- **WhatsApp,** where most Indian students and parents already are.
- **Student portal,** for logged-in current students.

## Turning conversations into admissions

A good admissions assistant does more than answer questions:

- Captures name, phone, course of interest and city.
- Scores intent, for example someone asking about fee payment deadlines is further along than someone asking about the campus.
- Sends qualified enquiries to counsellors with the conversation attached.
- Follows up with reminders about deadlines.

## Measuring success

Agree the measures before launch, so the next admissions season can build on this one:

- **Share of questions answered without staff.** The main efficiency measure.
- **Accuracy on the weekly review sample.** A counsellor checks a sample of answers against the source documents.
- **Enquiries captured,** and how many became applications and admissions.
- **Response time** for enquiries handed to counsellors.
- **Top unanswered questions,** which show where documents or website pages need improving.

The last measure is often the most valuable. It tells the institution exactly what prospective students want to know and cannot find.

## Accuracy and trust

Institutions cannot afford wrong information about fees or eligibility. Safeguards include:

- Answering only from approved documents.
- A test set of real questions from past seasons, checked before launch.
- Clear dates on fee and deadline information, updated as notices change.
- Human handover for complaints, disputes and personal cases.
- Regular review of unanswered questions to fill gaps.

## Languages

Students and parents often write in Hindi, English or a mix. Modern models handle this well, even when the source documents are in English.

## Privacy

Student data must be handled carefully. The assistant should collect only what admissions needs, store it securely, and follow the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. Private deployment options keep data within the institution's control.

## A rollout plan

1. **Collect and clean documents:** prospectus, fee notices, FAQs.
2. **Build and test** on real questions from last year's admissions.
3. **Launch on the website,** then WhatsApp.
4. **Review weekly** during admissions season.
5. **Extend to current students** after the season.

## Frequently asked questions

### Will it replace our admissions counsellors?

No. It removes repetitive questions so counsellors spend time on applicants who need guidance.

### How long does it take to launch?

A focused admissions assistant can be ready in four to six weeks, ideally before the season opens.

### Can it integrate with our admissions software?

Yes. Enquiries can be sent to your CRM or admissions system automatically.

### What if fees or dates change mid-season?

Update the source document and the assistant uses the new information immediately.

## Build an assistant for your institution

Turbo Bytes Consulting builds [AI applications](/services/ai-applications) for universities and colleges, including admissions and student support assistants. Institutions with sensitive data can deploy on [private infrastructure](/services/custom-llm).

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) to plan an assistant for your next admissions season.

posts.title: Core Web Vitals Explained for Business Owners
posts.excerpt: Core Web Vitals are Google's measures of how fast and stable your pages feel to real visitors. They affect rankings and enquiries. Here is what they mean in plain terms and what usually fixes them.
posts.content:
Core Web Vitals are three measurements Google uses to judge how a page feels to real visitors: how quickly the main content appears, how quickly the page responds when someone taps or clicks, and whether the layout jumps around while loading. Good scores support search rankings and, more importantly, keep impatient visitors on the page long enough to enquire.

## The three measurements

### Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): loading

How long it takes for the biggest visible element, usually the main image or headline, to appear. Google considers under 2.5 seconds good.

**In plain terms:** does the page look ready quickly?

### Interaction to Next Paint (INP): responsiveness

How long the page takes to respond visibly after someone taps a button, opens a menu or types in a form. Under 200 milliseconds is good.

**In plain terms:** does the page react immediately, or does it feel stuck?

### Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): stability

How much content moves around unexpectedly while the page loads, such as a button jumping just as someone tries to tap it. A score under 0.1 is good.

**In plain terms:** does the page stay still?

## Why business owners should care

- **Search visibility.** Page experience is one of the signals Google uses, and speed affects how much of your site Google crawls.
- **Enquiries.** Visitors on mobile networks leave slow pages before reading your offer.
- **Credibility.** A site that jumps around or lags feels unreliable, which matters when you are selling expertise.

## How to check your scores

1. **Google Search Console:** the Core Web Vitals report shows real-user data for your pages, grouped as good, needs improvement or poor.
2. **PageSpeed Insights:** enter any URL for a detailed report and suggestions.
3. **Test on a real phone** on mobile data, not just office Wi-Fi.

## The usual culprits and fixes

| Problem | Typical cause | Usual fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slow loading (LCP) | Huge hero images, slow hosting, heavy themes | Compress and resize images, modern formats, better hosting, preload the main image |
| Sluggish response (INP) | Too much JavaScript, chat widgets, trackers | Remove unused scripts, delay non-essential widgets |
| Layout jumps (CLS) | Images without set sizes, late-loading banners and fonts | Reserve space for images and ads, load fonts properly |

Third-party scripts, such as chat widgets, heatmaps and multiple analytics tags, are often the biggest hidden cost. Each one should earn its place.

## Platform matters

Modern frameworks such as Next.js handle image optimisation, font loading and code splitting by default, which makes good scores easier to achieve and keep. Plugin-heavy WordPress sites can score well too, but need more care. See [Next.js vs WordPress](/blog/nextjs-vs-wordpress-for-a-business-website-in-2026).

## Keeping scores good over time

Sites rarely get slow in one step. They get slow one addition at a time. A few habits prevent that:

- **Set an image rule.** Every uploaded image is resized and compressed, ideally automatically by the CMS or framework.
- **Approve every new script.** Before adding a chat widget, pixel or heatmap, ask what decision it will inform and remove it if nobody uses the data.
- **Check monthly.** Glance at the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console once a month, and after any significant change.
- **Test new pages on mobile data** before publishing landing pages for campaigns.
- **Give one person ownership** of site performance, whether in-house or your web partner.

These habits cost little and keep the site fast for years.

## What good looks like

For a B2B service site, aim for all three metrics in the good range on mobile for your key pages: home, services, contact and top blog posts. Check again after every redesign or major plugin change.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do Core Web Vitals guarantee better rankings?

No. Relevant, helpful content matters more. But between similar pages, better experience helps, and it improves conversion regardless.

### Why do lab tests and Search Console differ?

Lab tests simulate one device; Search Console reflects real visitors on many devices and networks. Search Console is what Google uses.

### How long do improvements take to show?

Search Console reports use a rolling 28-day window, so improvements appear gradually over about a month.

### Can we fix this without a redesign?

Often yes. Image optimisation, script clean-up and hosting changes fix most problems.

## Make your site fast

Turbo Bytes Consulting builds fast, stable [websites and web applications](/services/web-development), and audits existing sites for speed. Planning a rebuild? Start with our [website redesign checklist](/blog/website-redesign-checklist-for-b2b-companies).

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) and we will review your key pages.

posts.title: Automating Approvals: Purchase, Leave and Expense Workflows
posts.excerpt: Approvals are where growing companies lose days without noticing. Automating purchase, leave and expense workflows with clear limits speeds decisions and gives the founder their time back.
posts.content:
Automating approvals means every purchase request, leave application or expense claim follows written rules: it goes to the right person based on amount, department and type, reminds them if it waits too long, lets them approve on their phone, and records who decided what and when. The result is faster decisions, fewer interruptions for senior people, and a clean audit trail.

In many growing companies, approvals still happen by email, WhatsApp or a signature on paper. Requests get lost, people chase each other, and the founder approves small amounts because nobody wrote down who else can.

## The three most common workflows

### Purchase requests

1. An employee raises a request with item, quantity, estimated cost and supplier.
2. The system routes it by amount: department head up to one limit, finance above it, the founder only for large or unusual purchases.
3. Approved requests become purchase orders automatically.
4. Goods receipt and supplier invoice are matched against the order before payment.

### Leave

1. The employee applies on their phone, seeing their balance first.
2. The manager approves, with a view of who else is on leave that week.
3. HR records update automatically, and payroll receives the data at month end.

### Expenses

1. The employee photographs the receipt and submits a claim.
2. Policy rules check limits by category and grade.
3. The manager approves, finance verifies, and the payment is scheduled.

## Designing the rules

The software is the easy part. The rules are where the value lies.

| Decision | Write down |
| --- | --- |
| Who approves | By role, not by name, so rules survive staff changes |
| Limits | Amount bands per role and category |
| Delegation | Who approves when the approver is on leave |
| Escalation | What happens after 24 or 48 hours without action |
| Exceptions | Emergency purchases, single-supplier items, over-budget requests |

Start with the rules you actually follow today, then tighten them. Approval limits alone often remove most of the requests that reach the founder.

## Features that matter

- **Mobile approval** with one tap, including from WhatsApp or email notifications.
- **Reminders and escalation** so nothing waits silently.
- **Budget visibility**: the approver sees how much of the budget is already committed.
- **Audit trail**: who approved, when, and with what comment.
- **Reports**: average approval time, requests by department, spending against budget.
- **Integration** with Tally or your accounting system for purchase orders and payments. See our guide to [Tally integration](/blog/tally-integration-connecting-your-accounts-to-your-operations-software).

## What changes after automation

Companies that automate approvals usually notice three shifts within a few months:

- **Faster cycles.** Purchase requests that took days to clear now take hours, because approvers act from their phones and reminders stop requests being forgotten.
- **Fewer interruptions for senior people.** Most requests fall within limits and never reach the founder or finance head. Their inbox fills only with genuine exceptions.
- **Better spending control.** Because approvers see committed spend against budget before deciding, overspends surface at the request stage rather than at month end.

There is also a cultural effect. When rules are clear and applied consistently, people stop lobbying individuals for approval, and managers gain confidence to decide within their limits.

## Build, buy or configure

Many HR and expense tools include approval workflows, and they suit standard needs. A custom workflow makes sense when your approval rules are complex, when approvals must connect to your own operations software, or when you want one approval inbox across purchase, sales discounts, credit limits and HR. Our framework for [build, buy or extend decisions](/blog/build-buy-or-extend-choosing-software-for-a-100-person-company) applies here.

## Getting adoption

- Launch one workflow at a time, starting with the most painful.
- Stop accepting approvals by other channels once the system is live.
- Show the approval time report at the monthly review; visible speed builds support.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long does it take to set up approval workflows?

A single custom workflow with mobile approvals typically takes three to six weeks. Several connected workflows are delivered in phases.

### Can approvals happen on WhatsApp?

Notifications and one-tap approval links can be sent over WhatsApp Business, with the decision recorded in the system.

### What if an approver leaves the company?

Rules based on roles rather than names route requests to the new person automatically.

### Does this help with audits?

Yes. Every decision is recorded with time, person and comment, which auditors value.

## Speed up decisions in your business

Turbo Bytes Consulting designs and builds approval workflows as part of our [business automation services](/services/business-automation), connected to your accounts and operations.

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) and tell us which approvals slow your team down.

posts.title: Software for Logistics and Distribution Businesses
posts.excerpt: Distributors and logistics operators in Delhi NCR run on thin margins and fast decisions. The right software gives them live stock, accurate dispatch, dealer self-service and visibility of every rupee owed.
posts.content:
The most valuable software for logistics and distribution businesses covers four things: accurate, live inventory across warehouses; order management from dealer to dispatch; delivery tracking with proof of delivery; and a clear view of outstanding payments by customer. Connected to Tally and WhatsApp, these systems remove most of the calls and spreadsheets that consume a distributor's day.

Delhi NCR is one of India's largest distribution hubs, with warehouses along the expressways and in the industrial areas of Noida, Ghaziabad, Gurugram and Faridabad. Many distributors have grown to dozens of staff and hundreds of dealers while still coordinating by phone.

## Where time and money leak

- **Stock uncertainty.** Salespeople promise stock that is not there, or the warehouse holds slow-moving items nobody knows about.
- **Order entry.** Orders arrive by phone, WhatsApp and email, and are typed in by hand.
- **Dispatch planning** done on paper or in a spreadsheet each morning.
- **Delivery disputes** with no proof of what was delivered and when.
- **Collections.** Salespeople do not know which dealers are overdue.
- **Scheme management.** Discounts and schemes calculated manually, with errors.

## The core systems

### Inventory and warehouse

Barcode scanning at receipt and dispatch, stock by location and batch, reorder alerts, and slow-moving stock reports.

### Order management

Orders from salespeople, dealers and the office in one place, with automatic price and scheme calculation and stock reservation.

### Dispatch and delivery

Daily dispatch planning by route and vehicle, a driver app with delivery confirmation, photos and signatures, and automatic WhatsApp updates to customers.

### Dealer portal

Dealers place repeat orders, check balances and download invoices themselves, which cuts calls to the office.

### Collections and credit

Outstanding balances by dealer, credit limits enforced at order entry, and reminders for overdue payments.

## Integrations

| System | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Tally | Invoices, stock values and receivables stay consistent |
| WhatsApp Business | Order confirmations, dispatch updates, payment reminders |
| E-way bill and GST systems | Compliance for goods movement |
| Field sales app | Orders captured at the dealer's counter |

See our guides to [Tally integration](/blog/tally-integration-connecting-your-accounts-to-your-operations-software) and [building a field sales app](/blog/building-a-field-sales-app-for-your-team).

## Where to start

- **If stock is the problem:** start with inventory and barcodes.
- **If order errors are the problem:** start with order management and scheme rules.
- **If cash is the problem:** start with collections visibility and credit limits.

The first system should pay for itself within months through fewer errors, faster dispatch or better collections.

## What a typical day looks like after

Consider a distributor with 300 dealers and two warehouses. Before new systems, the morning started with a call list, a stock spreadsheet updated the previous evening, and a dispatch plan written on paper.

Afterwards:

- Dealer orders placed overnight on the portal are already priced, checked against credit limits and reserved against stock.
- The dispatch planner sees orders grouped by route and assigns vehicles on one screen.
- Drivers open their delivery list on the app, capture signatures and photos, and customers receive a WhatsApp confirmation automatically.
- By noon, the owner sees orders, dispatches and collections for the day on a dashboard, without asking anyone.

The team is the same size. The difference is that their time goes into exceptions and customers rather than re-typing and chasing.

## Measuring results

Before starting, record current order-to-dispatch time, stock accuracy at the last count, delivery disputes per month and days sales outstanding. Measure again three months after go-live.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can this work with our existing Tally setup?

Yes. Most distributors keep Tally for accounts and connect operational systems to it.

### Will our dealers use a portal?

Dealers who reorder regularly adopt portals quickly, especially when orders placed there are confirmed faster than by phone. A web link shared on WhatsApp works better than an app for most dealers.

### How long does implementation take?

A focused first module usually goes live in two to four months, with further modules added in phases.

### Do we need a full ERP instead?

Some distributors do well with a packaged ERP. Others need custom scheme, dealer and dispatch logic that packaged systems handle poorly. See [ERP: build, buy or customise](/blog/erp-for-manufacturing-smes-build-buy-or-customise).

posts.title: Why Data Quality Decides Whether AI Works
posts.excerpt: Most AI projects that disappoint were not let down by the model. They were let down by duplicate records, outdated documents and data nobody owned. Fixing that is a leadership task, not a technical one.
posts.content:
AI systems are only as reliable as the data they work from. A chatbot trained on outdated policies gives outdated answers; a forecast built on duplicate customer records predicts the wrong demand. For most mid-sized businesses, improving data quality delivers more AI value than choosing a better model, and it is a leadership responsibility because data problems are ownership problems.

## What poor data looks like in practice

- **Duplicates.** The same customer entered three times with different spellings in the CRM, Tally and a spreadsheet.
- **Outdated documents.** Four versions of a price list or policy in the shared drive, with no way to tell which is current.
- **Missing fields.** Orders without industry, region or source recorded, so analysis is impossible.
- **Inconsistent definitions.** Sales and finance count "revenue" or "active customer" differently.
- **Data in people's heads and inboxes.** Specifications, costing logic and customer history that were never written down.

## How each problem breaks AI

| Data problem | What the AI does |
| --- | --- |
| Outdated documents | Quotes the wrong policy or price confidently |
| Duplicates | Overcounts customers and distorts predictions |
| Missing fields | Cannot segment, forecast or personalise |
| Conflicting definitions | Produces numbers nobody trusts |
| Knowledge not written down | Has nothing to learn from |

The model is working exactly as designed in every case. The input is wrong.

## Why this is a leadership issue

Data quality degrades when nobody owns it. Each department keeps its own records to its own standards, and cross-department data belongs to no one. Only leadership can:

- Assign an owner to each key data set: customers, products, prices, policies.
- Agree one definition for each key metric.
- Make data entry part of how work is done, not an extra task.
- Fund clean-up as a project with an end date.

## A practical clean-up plan

1. **Pick the data your first AI use case needs.** Do not try to clean everything.
2. **Assign an owner** with authority to decide what is correct.
3. **Remove duplicates and archive superseded documents.**
4. **Fill critical missing fields** for active records.
5. **Fix the source.** Change forms and processes so the same problems do not return, for example mandatory fields and a single customer master.
6. **Measure.** Track duplicates, missing fields and document age monthly.

## An example from sales

A growing company wants an AI tool to identify which customers are likely to reorder, so salespeople can call them first. The data audit finds:

- The same customer appears under different names in the CRM and in Tally, so order history is split.
- A fifth of orders have no product category, so buying patterns are incomplete.
- "Active customer" means ordered in the last 90 days to sales, and invoiced in the financial year to accounts.

Built on this data, the model would underestimate loyal customers and misread demand. After three weeks of matching customer records, filling categories for the last two years of orders and agreeing one definition, the same model produces a list the sales team trusts and uses. The model did not change. The data did.

## Systems that keep data clean

Much bad data comes from the same information being typed into several places. Integrating systems, so that a customer is created once and shared, prevents a large share of quality problems. See [Tally integration](/blog/tally-integration-connecting-your-accounts-to-your-operations-software) and [build, buy or extend decisions](/blog/build-buy-or-extend-choosing-software-for-a-100-person-company).

## How to know you are ready for AI

- You can name the owner of the data your AI use case depends on.
- The current version of every key document is clearly marked.
- Key records have the fields the use case needs.
- You can describe how the data will be kept current after launch.

If you cannot tick these, start with the data. The AI project will be faster and more successful for it.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can AI clean our data for us?

Partly. AI tools can find likely duplicates and suggest corrections, but a person who owns the data must confirm them.

### How long does a data clean-up take?

For the data behind one use case, typically two to six weeks alongside normal work.

### Should we wait until all our data is clean?

No. Clean what the first use case needs, launch, and expand from there.

### Who should own data quality?

Each data set should have a business owner, such as the sales head for customers, supported by whoever manages your systems.

## Get your data ready

Turbo Bytes Consulting's [Business Diagnostic](/services) reviews data readiness before any AI investment, and our [AI applications](/services/ai-applications) work begins with a data review.

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) to discuss which data your first AI project needs.

posts.title: App Store Approval: What Delays Launches and How to Avoid It
posts.excerpt: App store review is the last step before launch and the one most teams underestimate. Most rejections are predictable and avoidable with a little preparation.
posts.content:
App launches are most often delayed at store review by predictable issues: incomplete store listings, missing privacy disclosures, login-only apps without test accounts for reviewers, broken features on the reviewer's device, and business apps that look like web pages wrapped in an app. Preparing for these before submission usually turns review into a formality rather than a setback.

## How review works

**Apple App Store** reviews every app and update manually. Reviewers test on real devices and check against Apple's guidelines.

**Google Play** uses automated checks plus human review for some apps. New developer accounts face extra requirements, including closed testing with real testers before production release.

Both reviews can take from a day to a week, and a rejection restarts the clock.

## The most common reasons business apps are rejected

### 1. Reviewers cannot log in

If your app requires an account, reviewers need working test credentials and any instructions to reach the main features. Missing or expired test accounts are among the most frequent causes of rejection.

### 2. Privacy disclosures do not match the app

Both stores require you to declare what data the app collects and why. If the app requests location or camera access, the declaration and the permission prompts must explain the purpose clearly.

### 3. Crashes or broken features

Reviewers test on devices and operating system versions you may not have tested. Any crash or dead button is grounds for rejection.

### 4. Minimal functionality

Apps that simply wrap a website, or offer very little, may be rejected for providing limited value. Business apps should use native capabilities, such as offline access, camera or notifications, meaningfully.

### 5. Incomplete listing

Missing screenshots, placeholder text, a missing support URL or a privacy policy link that does not work.

### 6. Account deletion

Apps that let users create accounts must also let them request account deletion from within the app.

### 7. Payments

Digital goods and subscriptions sold within an app often must use the store's billing. Physical goods and business services usually may use your own payment gateway. Get this right before building payments.

## Internal business apps

Apps only for your staff can avoid public review:

- **Apple:** distribution through Apple Business Manager as a custom app, or enterprise programmes where eligible.
- **Google:** managed Google Play for organisations, or direct installation on company devices.

Choose the route early, because it affects accounts and build settings.

## Pre-submission checklist

- [ ] Developer accounts in your company's name, with access for your developer
- [ ] Test account and reviewer notes prepared
- [ ] Privacy policy published and linked
- [ ] Data safety and privacy declarations completed accurately
- [ ] Permission prompts explain their purpose
- [ ] Tested on older and newer devices and OS versions
- [ ] Screenshots and descriptions for each required device size
- [ ] Account deletion available if accounts can be created
- [ ] Support contact and URL working
- [ ] Google Play closed testing completed if required for your account

## Updates after launch

Review does not end at launch. Every update goes through the stores again, and both Apple and Google regularly raise requirements, such as new privacy declarations or minimum operating system targets. To keep updates smooth:

- **Release on a regular rhythm,** such as every two to four weeks, rather than in large, risky batches.
- **Use staged rollouts** on Google Play and phased releases on the App Store, so a problem reaches a small share of users first.
- **Keep test accounts valid permanently,** not just for the first submission.
- **Watch for policy emails** from both stores; deadlines for new requirements are usually announced months ahead.
- **Monitor crash reports** after each release and be ready to ship a fix quickly.

Budgeting for this ongoing work is part of the real cost of an app. See [mobile app development cost in India](/blog/mobile-app-development-cost-in-india-what-drives-the-price).

## Plan the timeline

Allow at least two weeks between feature completion and your public launch date for testing, store preparation and review. Announcing a launch date before approval is a common and avoidable source of embarrassment.

## Frequently asked questions

### Who should own the developer accounts?

Your company. Developers should be invited as team members, so you keep control of the app if you change partners.

### How long does Apple review take?

Often one to two days, but allow longer for first submissions and around major holidays.

### Can we update the app without review?

Store updates require review. Some content and configuration can change from your server without a new release, if the app is designed for it.

### What if we are rejected?

Read the reason carefully, fix it, and reply through the review system. Most rejections are resolved in one round.

## Launch without surprises

Turbo Bytes Consulting builds [mobile apps](/services/mobile-app-development) and handles store submission under your company's accounts. Choosing a framework? Read [React Native vs Flutter vs native](/blog/react-native-vs-flutter-vs-native-in-2026).

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) to plan your app and its launch.

posts.title: Fixed Price vs Time and Materials: Which Software Contract Protects You
posts.excerpt: Fixed price protects your budget when scope is clear. Time and materials protects flexibility when it is not. The safest contracts combine both, phase by phase.
posts.content:
A fixed-price software contract protects your budget when the scope is clearly defined and unlikely to change. A time-and-materials contract protects your flexibility when requirements will evolve. For most business software, the safest structure is a hybrid: a short paid discovery, then fixed prices for each defined phase, with a simple change process for anything new.

## Fixed price

You agree a scope and a price. The vendor carries the risk of taking longer than estimated.

**Protects you when:**

- Requirements are written, specific and agreed.
- The project is well understood, such as a website or a system similar to ones the vendor has built.
- Your budget is fixed and cannot stretch.

**Risks:**

- Vendors add contingency to cover uncertainty, so you may pay more than the work needs.
- Every change becomes a negotiation.
- If the vendor underestimates, quality can suffer as they try to protect their margin.
- Vague scope leads to disputes over what was included.

## Time and materials

You pay for the hours actually worked, usually against an estimate and a budget ceiling.

**Protects you when:**

- Requirements will emerge as users see the software.
- The work involves research, such as AI or complex integrations.
- You want to reprioritise frequently.

**Risks:**

- Costs can grow without firm controls.
- You carry the risk of inefficiency.
- It requires more involvement from you to steer priorities.

## Side by side

| Factor | Fixed price | Time and materials |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Budget certainty | High | Lower |
| Flexibility | Low | High |
| Who carries estimation risk | Vendor | You |
| Suits | Clear, stable scope | Evolving or uncertain scope |
| Your involvement needed | Moderate | Higher |
| Change handling | Change requests | Reprioritise the backlog |

## The hybrid that works

1. **Paid discovery, fixed fee (1 to 3 weeks).** Produces a specification, screen designs and estimates. See [what a requirements document should contain](/blog/what-a-software-requirements-document-should-contain-before-you-hire-a-developer).
2. **Phase 1, fixed price.** The clearly defined first release.
3. **Change requests.** Anything new is estimated and approved in writing before work starts.
4. **Later phases, fixed price or capped time and materials,** depending on how clear they are.
5. **Support retainer** after launch for maintenance and small improvements.

This gives you budget certainty for defined work and flexibility where it is genuinely needed.

## Where disputes usually come from

Most software contract disputes are not about the pricing model. They come from:

- **Unwritten assumptions.** The client assumed reports were included; the vendor assumed they were phase two.
- **Acceptance without criteria.** "Done" meant different things to each side.
- **Slow feedback.** The client took three weeks to review a milestone, the vendor's team moved on, and the schedule slipped.
- **Scope creep through small requests.** Dozens of minor changes agreed on calls, never priced, then questioned at invoice time.

Each has a simple remedy: a written scope with an explicit out-of-scope list, acceptance criteria per milestone, an agreed review turnaround, and a change log that both sides see weekly. These matter more than whether the contract says fixed price or time and materials.

## Contract terms that protect you under either model

- **Milestone payments** tied to working software you have accepted, not to calendar dates.
- **Acceptance criteria** for each milestone.
- **Source code in your repository** throughout.
- **Intellectual property** transferred on payment.
- **Warranty** for defects for a period after go-live.
- **Budget caps and weekly reporting** for time-and-materials work.
- **Exit clause** with handover obligations.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is fixed price cheaper?

Not necessarily. It includes the vendor's contingency. It is more predictable, which is often what matters.

### What is a reasonable change request process?

A short written description, an estimate of cost and time, and your approval before work starts. Small changes can be pooled and reviewed weekly.

### How much should discovery cost?

Typically a small share of the expected project cost. It usually saves more than it costs by reducing uncertainty in the main quote.

### Which model suits AI projects?

Time and materials with a cap for the proof of concept, then fixed price for the production build once accuracy and scope are known.

## Contract for success

Turbo Bytes Consulting works on a discovery-then-fixed-phase model for [custom software](/services/custom-software-development) and [AI applications](/services/ai-applications). For budgeting, see [custom software costs in India](/blog/how-much-does-custom-software-development-cost-in-india-in-2026).

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) and we will recommend the right structure for your project.

posts.title: On-Premise LLM Hardware: What You Actually Need
posts.excerpt: Running a language model on your own servers is now practical for mid-sized businesses. The hardware you need depends on model size, number of users and how fast answers must arrive, not on headlines about data centres.
posts.content:
For most business uses, such as answering questions from company documents, drafting and summarising, an on-premise LLM runs well on a single server with one modern GPU carrying enough memory for the chosen model. The key number is GPU memory: it decides which model sizes you can run and how many people can use the system at once. Larger deployments add GPUs as usage grows.

Businesses in professional services, finance, healthcare and engineering increasingly want AI without sending client data to outside providers. Open models have improved to the point where many business tasks no longer need the largest hosted models, which makes on-premise deployment realistic.

## The four things that decide hardware

### 1. Model size

Models are described by their number of parameters: a few billion for small models, tens of billions for medium ones, and far more for the largest. Larger models reason better but need more memory. Many retrieval-based business tasks run well on small and medium models.

### 2. Quantisation

Quantisation stores the model's numbers with lower precision, which shrinks memory needs substantially with a modest loss of quality. Most on-premise business deployments use quantised models. The right level is chosen by testing accuracy on your own questions.

### 3. Concurrent users

Each active request needs memory for its context, the text the model is reading and writing. Ten people asking questions at the same moment need more headroom than one. Most internal assistants see far fewer simultaneous requests than total users.

### 4. Context length

Retrieval systems send the question plus relevant document passages. Longer contexts need more memory per request. Precise retrieval keeps contexts short, which improves both speed and accuracy.

## The components

| Component | What matters | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPU | Memory first, then speed | Decides which models fit and how many users are served |
| CPU | Moderate | Handles retrieval, pre-processing and the application |
| System RAM | Generous | Loading models, document indexes, caching |
| Storage | Fast SSD | Models, indexes and documents load quickly |
| Network | Standard office or data-centre networking | Serving users across the office |
| Power and cooling | GPU servers draw significant power | Plan the location, not just the purchase |

## Sizing examples

These illustrate the shape of decisions, not exact specifications, which change as models and hardware evolve.

**Small team knowledge assistant (up to about 50 users, light concurrent use).** A workstation-class machine with one GPU carrying a moderate amount of memory, running a small or medium quantised model. Suitable for policy, HR and document question-answering.

**Department or company-wide assistant (a few hundred users).** A server with a data-centre or high-memory GPU, running a medium model with room for several simultaneous requests, plus a separate machine or container for retrieval and the application.

**Multiple applications and heavier workloads.** Two or more GPUs, possibly different models for different tasks, such as a small fast model for classification and a larger one for complex drafting, with load balancing.

## Private cloud as an alternative

If buying and housing hardware is impractical, the same open models can run on GPU servers rented in a cloud account your company owns. Data stays in your account, you avoid capital cost, and capacity can scale up or down. Many businesses start in private cloud to prove the use case, then move on-premise once usage is steady.

## Before you buy anything

1. **Choose the use case** and build a test set of real questions.
2. **Test candidate models** on rented hardware or a trial machine.
3. **Pick the smallest model and quantisation** that meets your accuracy bar.
4. **Estimate concurrent use** from how people work, not total headcount.
5. **Size hardware with headroom** for growth, then buy.

This avoids the two common mistakes: buying far more than needed, or buying hardware that cannot run the model your accuracy test requires.

## Running it well

- Monitor GPU memory, response times and errors.
- Keep models and software updated, testing accuracy after each change.
- Back up document indexes and configuration.
- Restrict access by user and department, as you would any system holding sensitive information.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is on-premise AI as good as the best hosted models?

For broad reasoning, the largest hosted models are still ahead. For focused business tasks using your own documents, well-chosen open models often perform comparably, especially with good retrieval.

### Can we start small and upgrade later?

Yes. Design the application so the model can be swapped or scaled without rebuilding it.

### Who maintains the system?

Either your IT team with documentation and training, or a support agreement with the partner who built it.

### How does this compare in cost with hosted APIs?

With steady, high usage, on-premise can cost less over time. With light or unpredictable usage, hosted or private cloud is usually cheaper. See [what it costs to build an LLM application](/blog/what-it-costs-to-build-an-llm-powered-application-in-india).

Try our [knowledge portal demo](/ai-knowledge-portal.html) to see the kind of system this hardware supports.

[Book a 30-minute scoping call](/book-consultation) and we will size a deployment for your use case.
